# Chapter 7: Local Asymptotic Normality

## 7.1 Introduction

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Summary

1. Reparameterize locally using $\theta+h/\sqrt n$.
2. Assume differentiability in quadratic mean.
3. Obtain the quadratic likelihood expansion $h^T\Delta_{n,\theta}-\frac12h^TI_\theta h+o_{P_\theta}(1)$.
4. Recognize this as the likelihood-ratio form of a Gaussian location experiment.
5. Match limiting procedures in the original experiments to procedures in the Gaussian experiment.
6. Use the Gaussian experiment to understand maximum likelihood, local alternatives, testing, estimation, and asymptotic efficiency.
7. Abstract the likelihood expansion into the general definition of LAN for non-i.i.d. and dependent models.

The local behavior of a regular statistical model is asymptotically summarized by the central sequence $\Delta_{n,\theta}$ and the Fisher information $I_\theta$.

Locally, the original model behaves like observing $X\sim N(h,I_\theta^{-1})$.

:::

- A **sample** $X_1, \dots, X_n$ is from a **distribution** $P_\theta$ on a measurable space $(\mathcal X, \mathcal A)$ indexed by a **parameter** $\theta$ that ranges over an open subset $\Theta$ of $\mathbb R^k$
    - a full **observation** comes from $P_\theta^n$ (i.e., $n$ copies of $P_\theta$) (implies iid)
    - the **statistical model** is the collection of probability measures $\{P_\theta^n : \theta \in \Theta \}$ on **sample space** $(\mathcal X^n, \mathcal A^n)$
- A **statistical experiment** is a specification of the distribution of the data for every possible value of the parameter; a distribution corresponds to a specific parameter value, the experiment allows for all distributions permitted by a given model.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A sequence of statistical experiments is **locally asymptotically normal** when, after an appropriate local reparameterization, its likelihood-ratio process has the same asymptotic quadratic form as the likelihood-ratio process of a Gaussian location experiment.

:::

i.e., we are going to show that :

$$
\{P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n:h\in\mathbb R^k\} \approx \{N(h,I_{\theta_0}^{-1}):h\in\mathbb R^k\}
$$

- when $n$ is large and $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$ is smooth in the parameter

---

## 7.2 Expanding the Likelihood

### Local re-parameterization

- Fix parameter value $\theta_0$
- Define the **local parameter** $h=\sqrt n(\theta-\theta_0)$.
    - Equivalently, parameter values near $\theta_0$ can be written as $\theta=\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$.
    - So we can rewrite $P_\theta^n$ as  $P_{\theta_0+h/\sqrt n}^n$.
    - When $\theta_0$ is an interior point of $\Theta$, every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^k$ corresponds to a valid parameter $\theta_0+h/\sqrt n\in\Theta$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

---

### Heuristic likelihood expansion

- $p_\theta$ is a density of $P_\theta$ with respect to some measure $\mu$
- log-likelihood $\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$
    - the score function is $\dot \ell_\theta (x)= \partial \ell_\theta(x)/\partial \theta$
    - the second derivative is  $\ddot \ell_\theta (x) = \partial \dot \ell_\theta (x) /\partial \theta$

**Heuristic Taylor expansion:**

- assume parameter is one-dimensional
- assume $\ell_\theta(x)$ is twice differentiable with respect to $\theta$
- $\log\dfrac{p_{\theta+h}}{p_\theta}(x)=\ell_{\theta + h}(x) - \ell_{\theta}(x)$

Take a Taylor expansion of the first term, subtract the second, then:

$$
\log\dfrac{p_{\theta+h}}{p_\theta}(x)=h\dot\ell_\theta(x)+\frac12h^2\ddot\ell_\theta(x)+o_x(h^2).
$$

Summing the expansion over the sample and substituting the local shift $h/\sqrt n$ gives, under suitable regularity conditions,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}}{p_\theta}(X_i)
&=\frac{h}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\dot\ell_\theta(X_i)
+\frac{h^2}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ddot\ell_\theta(X_i)
+o_{P_\theta}(1)\\
&=h\Delta_{n,\theta}-\frac12h^2I_\theta+o_{P_\theta}(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

With:

- Under standard regularity conditions, the score has mean zero, $P_\theta\dot\ell_\theta=0$, and the Fisher information is

  $$
  I_\theta=P_\theta\dot\ell_\theta\dot\ell_\theta^T=-P_\theta\ddot\ell_\theta.
  $$

- The first term is random and asymptotically normal:

  $$
  \Delta_{n,\theta}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\dot\ell_\theta(X_i)\rightsquigarrow N(0,I_\theta)
  $$

  by the central limit theorem.
- The second term converges by the law of large numbers to the deterministic quadratic penalty $-\frac12h^2I_\theta$.

### Differentiability in quadratic mean {#sec-differentiability-quadratic-mean}

- The model $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta$ if there exists a measurable vector function $\dot\ell_\theta$ such that:

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
<span id="eq-differentiability-quadratic-mean"></span>

$$
(7.1) \qquad \int\left[\sqrt{p_{\theta+h}}-\sqrt{p_\theta}-\frac12h^T\dot\ell_\theta\sqrt{p_\theta}\right]^2\,d\mu=o(\|h\|^2), \qquad h\to0.
$$

:::

that is, when we move the parameter from $\theta$ to $\theta+h$ the **square-root density** changes approximately linearly in $h$.

When pointwise differentiation is valid, $\dot\ell_\theta(x)=  \frac{2}{\sqrt{p_\theta(x)}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \sqrt{p_\theta (x)} =\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(x)$.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 7.2 {#theorem-lan-iid}

Extending beyond one dimension:

- Suppose $\Theta$ is open and the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta$.

Then:

- $P_\theta\dot\ell_\theta=0$,
- the Fisher information matrix $I_\theta=P_\theta\dot\ell_\theta\dot\ell_\theta^T$ exists,
- and for every sequence $h_n\to h$:

$$
\log\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_{\theta+h_n/\sqrt n}(X_i)}{p_\theta(X_i)}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nh_n^T\dot\ell_\theta(X_i)-\frac12h_n^TI_\theta h_n+o_{P_\theta}(1).
$$

Differentiability in quadratic mean at $\theta$ implies the quadratic likelihood expansion above, and hence the i.i.d. sequence of experiments is LAN at $\theta$.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 7.6

A sufficient condition for differentiability in quadratic mean:

- Suppose $\theta\mapsto s_\theta(x) =\sqrt{p_\theta(x)}$ is continuously differentiable for every $x$
- the elements of $I_\theta=\int(\dot p_\theta/p_\theta)(\dot p_\theta/p_\theta)^Tp_\theta\,d\mu$ are well defined and continuous in $\theta.$

Then: the model $\theta \mapsto \sqrt{p_\theta (x)}$ is differentiable in quadratic mean (7.1) with score $\dot\ell_\theta=\dot p_\theta/p_\theta$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 7.7: Exponential families

Most exponential families are differentiable in quadratic mean when parameterized smoothly away from the boundary of the natural parameter space.

Exponential family model:

$$
p_\theta(x)=d(\theta)h(x)e^{Q(\theta)^Tt(x)}.
$$

- The score is $\dot \ell_\theta (x) = Q'_\theta \left( t(x) - \text{E}_\theta t(X)\right).$
- The Fisher information: $I_\theta = Q_\theta ' \text{cov}_\theta t(X) \left(Q_\theta '\right)^T$
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 7.8: Location models

Location model $\{f(x-\theta):\theta\in\mathbb R\}$.

If $f$ is positive and continuously differentiable and has finite Fisher information for location, then the model is differentiable in quadratic mean.

- The Fisher information: $I_f=\int \left(\dfrac{f'}{f}\right)^2(x) f(x)\,dx$ for every $\theta$
- The score is $\dot\ell_\theta(x)=-\{f'/f\}(x-\theta)$.

The Laplace location model is also differentiable in quadratic mean, even though the log density is not differentiable at $x=\theta$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Example 7.9: Uniform distribution counterexample

- The family of uniform distributions on $[0,\theta]$ is nowhere differentiable in quadratic mean.
- For the uniform model, $P_{\theta+h}(p_\theta=0)=h/(\theta+h)$, which is only $O(h)$.
    - differentiability in quadratic mean would require probability mass outside the support of $P_\theta$ to be $o(h^2)$.
:::

## 7.3 Convergence to a normal experiment

- Suppose the limit experiment consists of observing one observation of  $X\sim N(h,I_\theta^{-1})$.

Its log likelihood ratio relative to $h=0$ is:

$$
\log \dfrac{ dN(h,I_\theta^{-1})}{dN(0,I_\theta^{-1})}(X)=h^TI_\theta X-\frac12h^TI_\theta h.
$$

- This has the sort of the same quadratic form as the LAN expansion in 7.2 $h^T\Delta_{n,\theta}-\frac12h^TI_\theta h$.

- Suppose $T_n$ is a statistic in the local experiment and has a limiting distribution under every local parameter $h$.
- The convergence of experiments means that the family of limiting distributions of $T_n$ can be reproduced by a statistic in the Gaussian limit experiment.
- Thus asymptotic properties of procedures in the original model can be studied through procedures in the Gaussian experiment.

- A **randomized statistic** in the limit experiment has the form $T=T(X,U)$, where $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ is independent of $X$.
- Randomization is included to ensure that every possible limiting conditional distribution can be represented.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 7.10 {#theorem-normal-limit-experiment}

Representation theorem (in the limit experiment)

- Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta$ and $I_\theta$ is nonsingular.
- Let $T_n$ be statistics in the local experiments $\{P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n:h\in\mathbb R^k\}$, and suppose $T_n$ converges in distribution under every $h$.
- Then there exists a randomized statistic $T$ in the Gaussian experiment $\{N(h,I_\theta^{-1}):h\in\mathbb R^k\}$ having the same limiting distribution under every $h$.
:::

The proof combines joint convergence with the central sequence, contiguity, Le Cam’s third lemma, and a representation of conditional distributions using randomization.

### Lemma 7.11

Given a joint distribution $(S,\Delta)$, one can construct a measurable randomized function $T(\Delta,U)$ such that $(T(\Delta,U),\Delta)$ has the same distribution as $(S,\Delta)$.

---

## 7.4 Maximum likelihood

- Chapter 5 shows ML estimators in smooth parametric models are asymptotically normal
- By [Theorem 7.10](#theorem-normal-limit-experiment), every sequence of statistics in the local experiments $\{P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n:h\in\mathbb R^k\}$ is matched in the limit by a statistic in the normal experiment.
- Also (not following directly from this theorem) a sequence of ML estimators is typically matched by the ML estimator in the limit experiment.
    - The ML estimator of $h$ in the Gaussian experiment $N(h,I_\theta^{-1})$ is $X$ (the mean of a sample size one), normally distributed
    - This suggests that the local maximum likelihood estimator $\widehat h_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)$ should converge to $X$ under $h = 0$
    - i.e., for an interior parameter under suitable regularity conditions, $\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)\rightsquigarrow N(0,I_\theta^{-1})$.
- LAN therefore explains the asymptotic normality and asymptotic optimality of maximum likelihood estimators through the corresponding properties of maximum likelihood in the Gaussian experiment.
- LAN alone is not sufficient to prove this result; additional uniformity and consistency conditions are needed, see also conditions of Theorem 5.39.

### Constrained parameter spaces

- Let $H_n=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ be the local parameter space.
- If $H_n\to H$, the limiting maximum likelihood estimator maximizes the Gaussian likelihood over $H$.
- Equivalently, it is the projection of $X$ onto $H$ in the Fisher-information metric $d(x,y)=(x-y)^TI_{\theta_0}(x-y)$.
- If $H=\mathbb R^k$, the projection is simply $X$.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 7.12

- Suppose the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$,
- $I_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular,
- the log densities satisfy the stated local Lipschitz condition,
- $\widehat\theta_n$ is consistent,
- and $H_n=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ converges to a nonempty convex set $H$.

Then $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ converges in distribution to the projection of a standard normal vector onto $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H$.

Thus boundary restrictions can produce non-normal projected-Gaussian limiting distributions. ([portmanteau lemma](chapter-2.qmd#lemma-portmanteau) used in proof)

:::

**Proof.**

- Let $G_n=\sqrt n(\mathbb P_n-P_{\theta_0})$ be the empirical process, and define the local maximum likelihood estimator $\widehat h_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0).$
- The goal is to show that $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}\widehat h_n$ converges to the projection of a standard normal vector onto the limiting local parameter space $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H.$
1. **Step 1: Obtain a uniform quadratic approximation to the local log likelihood**
    - Under differentiability in quadratic mean and the Lipschitz condition, the log density is differentiable in $L_2(P_{\theta_0})$ at $\theta_0$, with derivative $\dot\ell_{\theta_0}$.
    - Also, the expected log likelihood has a second-order expansion at $\theta_0$ with curvature matrix $-I_{\theta_0}$.
    - Therefore, for every fixed $M<\infty$, $\sup_{|h|\leq M}\left|n\mathbb P_n\log\frac{p_{\theta_0+h/\sqrt n}}{p_{\theta_0}}-h^TG_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}+\frac12h^TI_{\theta_0}h\right|\overset{P_{\theta_0}}\longrightarrow0.$
    - Thus the local log likelihood is uniformly approximated by $h\mapsto h^TG_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-\frac12h^TI_{\theta_0}h.$
2. **Step 2: Restrict attention to a slowly expanding bounded set**
    - Consistency and the regularity assumptions imply that the MLE is $\sqrt n$consistent, so $\widehat h_n=O_{P_{\theta_0}}(1).$
    - Hence there exists a sequence $M_n\to\infty$ sufficiently slowly such that $P_{\theta_0}(|\widehat h_n|\leq M_n)\to1$ and the uniform quadratic approximation remains valid on the ball of radius $M_n$.
    - Therefore, with probability tending to one, $\widehat h_n$ maximizes the local likelihood over $H_n\cap{h:|h|\leq M_n},$ where $H_n=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0).$
    - These truncated sets still converge to $H$.
3. **Step 3: Bound the probability that the estimator lies in a closed set**
    - Fix an arbitrary closed set $F\subseteq\mathbb R^k.$
    - If $\widehat h_n\in F,$ then the maximum of the local log likelihood over $F\cap H_n$ must be at least as large as the maximum over all of $H_n$.
    - Hence $P_{\theta_0}(\widehat h_n\in F)\leq P_{\theta_0}\left(\sup_{h\in F\cap H_n}n\mathbb P_n\log\frac{p_{\theta_0+h/\sqrt n}}{p_{\theta_0}}\geq\sup_{h\in H_n}n\mathbb P_n\log\frac{p_{\theta_0+h/\sqrt n}}{p_{\theta_0}}\right).$
    - Using the uniform quadratic approximation, this is bounded by $P_{\theta_0}\left(\sup_{h\in F\cap H_n}\left[h^TG_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-\frac12h^TI_{\theta_0}h\right]\geq\sup_{h\in H_n}\left[h^TG_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-\frac12h^TI_{\theta_0}h\right]+o_P(1)\right).$
4. **Step 4: Complete the square**
    - For every $h,$ $h^TG_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-\frac12h^TI_{\theta_0}h=-\frac12\left|I_{\theta_0}^{-1/2}G_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}h\right|^2+\frac12\left|I_{\theta_0}^{-1/2}G_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}\right|^2.$
    - The last term does not depend on $h,$ so maximizing the quadratic expression is equivalent to minimizing distance.
    - Therefore, $P_{\theta_0}(\widehat h_n\in F)\leq P_{\theta_0}\left(\left|I_{\theta_0}^{-1/2}G_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}(F\cap H_n)\right|\leq\left|I_{\theta_0}^{-1/2}G_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H_n\right|+o_P(1)\right).$
    - Here, $|x-A|=\inf_{a\in A}|x-a|$ denotes the distance from $x$ to the set $A$.
5. **Step 5: Replace the varying sets by their limits**
    - Since $H_n\to H,$ Lemma 7.13 allows the distances to the varying sets to be replaced asymptotically by distances to the limiting sets.
    - Also, by the central limit theorem, $I_{\theta_0}^{-1/2}G_n\dot\ell_{\theta_0}\rightsquigarrow Z,$ where $Z\sim N(0,I_k).$
    - Hence the preceding probability is asymptotically bounded above by $P\left(|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}(F\cap H)|\leq|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H|\right).$
6. **Step 6: Interpret the event using projection**
    - Since $H$ is nonempty and convex, $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H$ is also nonempty, closed, and convex.
    - Therefore the projection $\Pi Z=\operatorname{argmin}*{u\in I*{\theta_0}^{1/2}H}|Z-u|$ exists and is unique.
    - If $|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}(F\cap H)|\leq|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H|,$ then the closest point to $Z$ in $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H$ must lie in $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}(F\cap H).$
    - Thus $P\left(|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}(F\cap H)|\leq|Z-I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}H|\right)\leq P(\Pi Z\in I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}F).$
7. **Step 7: Apply the portmanteau lemma**
    - For every closed set $F,$ the preceding argument gives the required limsup inequality.
    - By the closed-set formulation of the portmanteau lemma, $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}\widehat h_n\rightsquigarrow\Pi Z.$
    - Since $\widehat h_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0),$ we conclude that $I_{\theta_0}^{1/2}\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)\rightsquigarrow\Pi Z.$
    - If $\theta_0$ is an interior point, then typically $H=\mathbb R^k,$ so $\Pi Z=Z$ and the usual Gaussian limit is recovered.
    - If $\theta_0$ lies on the boundary, then $H$ is restricted, so the projection may have a nonnormal distribution.

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 7.13

- If $H_n\to H$ and $X_n\rightsquigarrow X$,
- then distances from $X_n$ to $H_n$ converge to the corresponding distance from $X$ to $H$, with related results for intersections with closed and open sets.

I.e.,

1. $\|X_n - H_n \| \rightsquigarrow \| X - H\|$
2. $\|X_n - H_n \cap F \| \ge \| X - H \cap F\| + o_P(1)$, for every closed set $F$
3. $\|X_n - H_n \cap G \| \le \| X - H \cap G\| + o_P(1)$, for every open set $G$
:::

**Proof.**

For (i)

1. Since $X_n\rightsquigarrow X$ and the map $x\mapsto |x-H|$ is continuous, then, by the [continuous mapping theorem](chapter-2.qmd#theorem-continuous-mapping): $\|X_n-H\|\rightsquigarrow \|X-H\|$
2. The set convergence $H_n\to H$ implies $\|X_n-H_n\|-\|X_n-H\|\overset{P}\to0$.
3. Then Slutsky’s lemma gives (i), $\|X_n-H_n\|\rightsquigarrow \|X-H\|.$

Parts (ii) and (iii) are one-sided approximations that follow from set convergence, distinction between closed and open set.

- $\|X_n-H_n\cap F\| \geq \|X_n-H\cap F\|+o_P(1)$ for closed $F$
    - If $F$ is closed and $h_n\in H_n\cap F$ with $h_n\to h$, then closedness implies $h\in F$, while set convergence implies $h\in H$. Hence $h\in H\cap F$. Therefore, $\|X_n-H_n\cap F\|$ cannot asymptotically be substantially smaller than $\|X_n-H\cap F\|$
- $\|X_n-H_n\cap G| \leq \|X_n-H\cap G\|+o_P(1)$ for open $G$.
    - If $G$ is open and $h\in H\cap G$, set convergence provides approximating points $h_n\in H_n$ with $h_n\to h$. Since $G$ is open, $h_n\in G$ eventually. Therefore, $\|X_n-H_n\cap G\|$ cannot asymptotically be substantially larger than $\|X_n-H\cap G\|$.

## 7.5 Limit distributions under alternatives

LAN implies under $P_\theta^n$

$$
\log\dfrac{dP^n_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}}{dP_\theta^n} \overset{\theta}{\rightsquigarrow} N(-\frac12h^TI_\theta h,h^TI_\theta h).
$$

Therefore $P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n$ and $P_\theta^n$ are mutually contiguous (see [Example 6.5](chapter-6.qmd#example-asymptotic-log-normality)).

- From [Theorem 7.2](#theorem-lan-iid), LAN gives the expansion:

$$
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n}{dP_\theta^n}=h^T\Delta_{n,\theta}-\frac12h^TI_\theta h+o_{P_\theta}(1),
$$

- where, under $P_\theta^n$, $\Delta_{n,\theta}\rightsquigarrow N(0,I_\theta).$
- Therefore, $h^T\Delta_{n,\theta}\rightsquigarrow N(0,h^TI_\theta h).$
- Adding the constant term gives:

$$
\log\frac{dP_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n}{dP_\theta^n}\rightsquigarrow N\left(-\frac12h^TI_\theta h,\,h^TI_\theta h\right).
$$

- Let $v=h^TI_\theta h.$ If $Z\sim N\left(-\frac12v,v\right)$,
    - then $e^Z>0$ almost surely and $E[e^Z]=e^{-v/2+v/2}=1.$
- Thus the limiting likelihood ratio is positive and has expectation one. By [Le Cam’s first lemma from 6.4](chapter-6.qmd#lemma-le-cam-first),

$$
P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n\triangleleft P_\theta^n.
$$

- Applying the same argument in the reverse direction gives

$$
P_\theta^n\triangleleft P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n.
$$

- Therefore, $P_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}^n\quad\text{and}\quad P_\theta^n$ are mutually contiguous.

### General scheme

- Suppose a statistic has an asymptotically linear expansion $\sqrt n(T_n-\mu_\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i)+o_{P_\theta}(1)$.
- The statistic and the log likelihood ratio have a joint multivariate normal limit under $P_\theta^n$.
- [Le Cam's third lemma, Example 6.7](chapter-6.qmd#lemma-le-cam-third) then gives the limiting distribution of $T_n$ under the local alternative $\theta+h/\sqrt n$.

The limiting covariance is unchanged, while the limiting mean is shifted according to the covariance between $\psi_\theta(X)$ and $h^T\dot\ell_\theta(X)$.

In particular, the mean shift is $P_\theta\psi_\theta\dot\ell_\theta^Th$.

This method is used to study the local asymptotic behavior and efficiency of estimators and tests.

---

## 7.6 Local Asymptotic Normality

The preceding results begin with i.i.d. observations, but LAN can be defined for general sequences of statistical models.

Let $\{P_{n,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}$ be a sequence of models.

::: {.callout-note title="Result"}
### Definition 7.14

The sequence $\{P_{n,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}$ is locally asymptotically normal at $\theta$ if there exist norming matrices $r_n$, a matrix $I_\theta$, and random vectors $\Delta_{n,\theta}$ such that $\Delta_{n,\theta}\rightsquigarrow N(0,I_\theta)$ under $P_{n,\theta}$, and for every sequence $h_n\to h$,

$\log\frac{dP_{n,\theta+r_n^{-1}h_n}}{dP_{n,\theta}}=h^T\Delta_{n,\theta}-\frac12h^TI_\theta h+o_{P_{n,\theta}}(1)$.

Here $r_n$ determines the local rate at which parameters approach $\theta$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 7.15: The i.i.d. case

If $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ is differentiable in quadratic mean, then $\{P_\theta^n:\theta\in\Theta\}$ is LAN with $r_n=\sqrt n I$.

The local experiments $\{P_{n,\theta+r_n^{-1}h}:h\in\mathbb R^k\}$ converge to $\{N(h,I_\theta^{-1}):h\in\mathbb R^k\}$ in the sense of Theorem 7.10.

:::
